questions.q: Some call religion a private matter, others a complete social order. How does the article itself describe the aim of Islam?
options: The winning of debates
Not quite. The article says: The individual’s discovery of God, which transforms him from within.
The preservation of old customs
Not quite. The article says: The individual’s discovery of God, which transforms him from within.
The building of a strong state
Not quite. The article says: The individual’s discovery of God, which transforms him from within.
The individual’s discovery of God, which transforms him from within
Yes. It addresses the individual, not society as a mass.
questions.rationale: “The aim of the religion of Islam is to discover our Creator… Islam addresses itself to the individual, not to society as a whole.”

questions.q: What were the first words of the infant Jesus, as the Quran relates them (19:30)?
options: “Take me to the temple”
Not quite. The article says: “I am God’s servant. He has given me the Book and made me a prophet”.
“Peace be upon this town”
Not quite. The article says: “I am God’s servant. He has given me the Book and made me a prophet”.
“I have come to rule”
Not quite. The article says: “I am God’s servant. He has given me the Book and made me a prophet”.
“I am God’s servant. He has given me the Book and made me a prophet”
Right. Spoken from the cradle, in his mother’s defence.
questions.rationale: “I am God’s servant. He has given me the Book and made me a prophet; He has made me blessed wherever I may be… He has made me dutiful toward my mother.”

questions.q: Why, according to the article, does the Quran return to the same themes again and again?
options: To make the book longer
Not quite. The article says: To engrave its message on the mind – what one loves, one gladly hears repeatedly, each time with new meaning.
Because its chapters were arranged by chance
Not quite. The article says: To engrave its message on the mind – what one loves, one gladly hears repeatedly, each time with new meaning.
Because earlier parts were forgotten
Not quite. The article says: To engrave its message on the mind – what one loves, one gladly hears repeatedly, each time with new meaning.
To engrave its message on the mind – what one loves, one gladly hears repeatedly, each time with new meaning
Well read. As a mother kisses her child again and again.
questions.rationale: “This has been done in order to engrave the message of the Quran in the minds of its readers… It is only natural that one should repeat something one loves or enjoys.”

questions.q: Two swallows’ mud nest collapsed with the eggs in it. What did they do next?
options: Took over another bird’s nest
Not quite. The article says: Found a rougher surface and rebuilt with mud mixed with grass and straw – a stronger nest.
Rebuilt the same nest in the same place
Not quite. The article says: Found a rougher surface and rebuilt with mud mixed with grass and straw – a stronger nest.
Found a rougher surface and rebuilt with mud mixed with grass and straw – a stronger nest
Yes. They corrected the cause of failure.
Abandoned the house altogether
Not quite. The article says: Found a rougher surface and rebuilt with mud mixed with grass and straw – a stronger nest.
questions.rationale: “Whereas the swallows had made their first nest just from mud, they made this one from a mixture of mud, grass and straw.”

questions.q: What does the article ask human beings to learn from the swallows?
options: Build homes only from natural materials
Not quite. The article says: After a failure, look for the reason and try again with better planning and harder work.
Depend on others in hard times
Not quite. The article says: After a failure, look for the reason and try again with better planning and harder work.
After a failure, look for the reason and try again with better planning and harder work
Correct. “It is a wise man who learns from his mistakes.”
Avoid tasks that may fail
Not quite. The article says: After a failure, look for the reason and try again with better planning and harder work.
questions.rationale: “If a bird or animal fails in some effort, it seeks to understand the reason for its failure. It does not simply give up… and rectifies its errors by harder work and better planning.”

questions.q: “Great things are done when men and mountains meet. This is not done by jostling in the street.” How does the article apply Blake’s lines?
options: Poets understand life better than leaders
Not quite. The article says: Great aims need patient assessment, sacrifice and long struggle – not slogans and processions.
Great aims need patient assessment, sacrifice and long struggle – not slogans and processions
Well reasoned. Noise is not work.
Crowds are needed for every great work
Not quite. The article says: Great aims need patient assessment, sacrifice and long struggle – not slogans and processions.
Great aims are reached only in the mountains
Not quite. The article says: Great aims need patient assessment, sacrifice and long struggle – not slogans and processions.
questions.rationale: “Just raising slogans or making speeches at big gatherings does not mean that any great work can be accomplished.”

questions.q: Abu Moosa al-Ashari said a judge should not decide until the truth is “as clear as day.” To whom does the article extend this rule?
options: Everyone who forms an opinion about another person – and if the matter is unclear, one should stay silent
Right. All will answer for their judgements.
Only to judges in courts
Not quite. The article says: Everyone who forms an opinion about another person – and if the matter is unclear, one should stay silent.
Only to rulers and governors
Not quite. The article says: Everyone who forms an opinion about another person – and if the matter is unclear, one should stay silent.
Only to witnesses
Not quite. The article says: Everyone who forms an opinion about another person – and if the matter is unclear, one should stay silent.
questions.rationale: “The principle that Abu Moosa laid down is applicable not only to judges but to every human being as well… if the truth is not ‘as clear as day’ then there is only one thing to do, and that is hold one’s peace.”

questions.q: The Hadith names three things displeasing to God. Which are they?
options: Sleeping, travelling and trading
Not quite. The article says: Idle talk, asking too many questions, and wasting money.
Silence, thrift and caution
Not quite. The article says: Idle talk, asking too many questions, and wasting money.
Idle talk, asking too many questions, and wasting money
Yes. Each makes a person a burden on society.
Laughing, eating and resting
Not quite. The article says: Idle talk, asking too many questions, and wasting money.
questions.rationale: “And three things cause Him immense displeasure: idle talk, asking too many questions and wasting money.”

questions.q: A village boy joined a queue for sweets at a school and was asked for his identity card. What does the story illustrate?
options: One should always carry documents
Not quite. The article says: The rewards of the Last Day are for those who qualified for them beforehand.
The rewards of the Last Day are for those who qualified for them beforehand
Exactly. Turning up at the window is not enough.
Village children are treated unfairly
Not quite. The article says: The rewards of the Last Day are for those who qualified for them beforehand.
Schools should feed all children
Not quite. The article says: The rewards of the Last Day are for those who qualified for them beforehand.
questions.rationale: “The rewards of that day will only be for those who have qualified for them… who, before the coming of that day, have shown themselves deserving of divine approval.”

questions.q: Man’s mind knows no boundaries, yet his physical existence is tightly limited. What does the article call the great test in this?
options: To think less and act more
Not quite. The article says: To find a balance between thinking and action, accepting one’s real limits.
To ignore the body’s limits
Not quite. The article says: To find a balance between thinking and action, accepting one’s real limits.
To avoid all ambition
Not quite. The article says: To find a balance between thinking and action, accepting one’s real limits.
To find a balance between thinking and action, accepting one’s real limits
Well read. Humility amid apparent greatness.
questions.rationale: “The greatest test of humanity is to discover a balance between thinking and action.”
